claims.text: The baseline is an as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state.
Stable intermetallic formation is responsible for performance limitations in the baseline alloy.
Mo addition is the proposed single intervention.
Mo addition promotes the formation of hard intermetallic compounds.
Mo induces lattice changes in the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
Mo promotes formation or stabilization of a protective passivation film.
Mo addition improves room-temperature compressive behavior relative to the as-processed baseline.
Mo addition improves corrosion resistance relative to the as-processed baseline.
Mo addition improves resistance to high-temperature oxidation relative to the as-processed baseline.
The modified alloy is intended to retain a density below 6 g/cm3.
Corrosion behavior is to be evaluated in 3.5% NaCl solution.
The relevant thermal boundary includes room temperature and an unspecified high-temperature oxidation condition.
The exposure time should be sufficient for passivation-film formation.
The amount of Mo required for optimal performance is unknown.
Other alloying elements may affect Mo-induced lattice changes and passivation-film formation.
A controlled series with varying Mo content can test the proposed effects on compression, corrosion, and oxidation.
The hypothesis is falsified if Mo addition fails to improve the three specified performance categories relative to the baseline.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis frames stable intermetallic formation as a source of performance limitations, but the proposed structural mediator is formation of hard intermetallic compounds. It does not explain how the newly formed intermetallics differ from, suppress, or mitigate the detrimental stable intermetallics.
